subject: Agriculture
title: Soil Degradation
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Soil Degradation.

hook.text: Punjab's soil was among India's richest in 1960. Sixty years of intensive cropping has depleted it.

buildup.text: Continuous rice-wheat rotation with heavy fertilizer mined the soil of micronutrients and organic matter.

discovery.text: Zinc, iron, and manganese deficiencies now limit yields. Farmers add more synthetic inputs to compensate.

twist.text: Burning rice stubble—common in Punjab—destroys organic matter that would have replenished the soil.

climax.text: Some areas now need twice the fertilizer for the same yield as 1970. The soil is running on empty.

punchline.text: The revolution squeezed the soil dry. Now it's pushing back.

quiz.question: Why do Punjab's farmers now need more fertilizer for the same yield?
options: Decades of intensive monoculture have depleted soil micronutrients and organic matter

details.summary: Decades of Green Revolution-style intensive farming have degraded soils across major agricultural regions through compaction, nutrient depletion, organic matter loss, and chemical contamination. This topic covers the soil health costs of intensification and emerging strategies for soil restoration.
details.whyItMatters: Soil degradation from intensive farming threatens the long-term productivity gains the Green Revolution achieved. In Punjab, India—the heartland of the wheat revolution—soil organic matter has declined by 50% and yields are now stagnating.
takeaways: Continuous monoculture and heavy fertilizer use have depleted soil organic matter by 30-50%
Rice-wheat rotation in South Asia has degraded soil structure and increased zinc deficiency
Yield stagnation in Green Revolution heartlands is increasingly linked to soil degradation

faq.question: How has intensive Green Revolution farming degraded soils?
faq.answer: Continuous monoculture depletes specific nutrients and breaks pest cycles. Heavy machinery compacts soil. Synthetic fertilizer without organic matter returns degrades soil biology. Flooded rice-wheat rotations destroy soil structure.

faq.question: Can degraded Green Revolution soils be restored?
faq.answer: Yes, through diversified rotations, cover crops, reduced tillage, organic amendments, and integrated nutrient management. India's zero-till wheat movement has improved soil health while maintaining yields. The challenge is changing farmer practices entrenched over decades of conventional management.
